title: Affect Theory
keyWorks: B. Massumi, Parables for the Virtual (2002)
S. Ahmed, The Cultural Politics of Emotion (2004)
S. Ahmed, The Promise of Happiness (2010)
S. Ahmed, Living a Feminist Life (2017)
summary: Affect theory is a strand of humanities thought from the 1990s–2010s that grew out of the philosophy of Spinoza and Deleuze. It looks at feelings not as something locked “inside” a person but as forces that pass through bodies, between people and through society. Brian Massumi studies affect as bodily intensity, while Sara Ahmed studies how emotions circulate and “stick” to people, things and words.
onEmotions: Massumi distinguishes affect from emotion. Affect is a pre-personal intensity: a bodily surge that happens before we have time to name it. Emotion is intensity that has already been “captured,” given a name and a place in the story we tell about ourselves. Sara Ahmed asks a different question: not “what is an emotion?” but “what do emotions do?” In her view, emotions do not belong to one person: they move between people, “stick” to objects, groups and words, and in doing so draw boundaries — who “we” are, who “they” are, what counts as a good life. For both, a feeling is neither a malfunction nor a purely private matter but a way in which the world touches us and we touch the world.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is one of the most understandable feelings of our time, and there is nothing shameful in feeling it. Brian Massumi describes contemporary culture as life under the sign of “threat”: a danger that has not yet happened, and may never happen, is already acting on the body now. He calls this an “affective fact” — a future that is felt as real in the present. The body responds to such signals before we have time to think them through, and anxiety becomes the general background of an era, not just your personal trait. This distinction can be a little freeing: anxiety passes through you the way weather passes through a city, but it does not exhaust who you are. And its intensity, for Massumi, is also an unformed energy that can find another channel.
anxiety.practice: Place your hand where anxiety lives in your body right now and ask yourself: what in this minute — not in the future — is it responding to?

fear.text: Fear is an ancient and necessary signal: it tells you that you might get hurt, and it deserves respect. Massumi emphasizes that fear happens first in the body: breath, muscles and heart react a split second before the thought “I’m afraid” appears. Sara Ahmed adds a social dimension: fear “shrinks” the body, makes it take up less space, avoid certain streets, give up space. And this shrinking is unevenly distributed: some are told from childhood “be careful,” others “the world is yours.” Seeing this means understanding that your fear is not only a personal weakness but also a trace of how the world has treated people like you. Then you can gently ask yourself what space fear has taken from you, and reclaim at least a small part of it.
fear.practice: Recall one place or activity that fear has trained you out of. What would be the smallest and safest step back — even just in your imagination?

quote.text: The skin is faster than the word.
quote.author: Brian Massumi

sadness.text: Sadness does not need to justify itself — it has a right to exist. In The Promise of Happiness, Sara Ahmed shows how society turns happiness into a duty: we are expected to be glad about the “right” things, and a sad person is seen as a problem to be fixed as quickly as possible. Ahmed suggests not rushing into such fixing. Unhappiness, in her view, can be a form of knowledge: sadness sometimes notices what general cheerfulness prefers not to see — injustice, loss, what doesn’t “add up” in life. Seen this way, your sadness is not a breakdown of mood but a sensitivity that is registering something. You can stay with it without hurrying to turn it into a smile, and listen to what it is saying.
sadness.practice: Complete the sentence: “Maybe my sadness is noticing that …” — and don’t rush to do anything about it.

grief.text: Grief is one of the most powerful experiences there is, and it doesn’t have to fit into any timeline or the right words. Massumi shows that intensity is always greater than its name: the word “grief” only partly captures what is happening in the body — the heaviness, the emptiness in the chest, the sudden waves. So it is normal if you cannot explain it. Sara Ahmed, drawing on Judith Butler, points out that society does not recognize all losses equally: some are mourned publicly, while others go unnoticed — for example, the loss of a friend, an animal, or a relationship that those around you did not consider “real.” From this point of view, your grief is real even if no one around you has confirmed it. It is evidence of a bond that mattered and still matters.
grief.practice: Name — to yourself or on paper — what you have lost, the way you feel it, not the way people usually talk about it.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and that pain says how much we need others. Sara Ahmed invites us to see feelings not as something locked inside an individual: emotions arise at the boundary between us and the world, and they themselves draw that boundary. In Queer Phenomenology she writes that space can be arranged “for” some bodies and not others — and then a person feels out of place, as if the world does not reach out to meet them. From this point of view, loneliness is not proof that something is wrong with you but sometimes a sign that there are few shapes around you that you fit into. Ahmed also reminds us of something else: those who feel “out of line” often find one another, and such a meeting changes the space itself.
loneliness.practice: Where do you feel “out of place,” and where even a little “in place”? Write down one example of each.

quote.text: Emotions are not simply “in” the individual or the social, but produce the very surfaces and boundaries that allow the individual and the social to be delineated as if they are objects.
quote.author: Sara Ahmed

anger.text: Anger is a legitimate feeling, especially when it responds to something truly unjust. Sara Ahmed came up with the figure of the “feminist killjoy”: the one who, at the shared festive table, notices a hurt or an inequality — and is immediately treated as the cause of the spoiled mood. Ahmed puts it this way: when you point out a problem, you become the problem. Her point is not that anger is always good but that anger often carries information others find uncomfortable to hear. This can relieve you of unnecessary guilt for “ruining the atmosphere.” Your anger is not necessarily destruction; sometimes it is a way of saying “something is wrong here” and refusing to pretend that everything is fine.
anger.practice: Ask your anger: what exactly is it pointing to — and what would you like others to finally hear?

quote.text: Does the feminist kill other people’s joy by pointing out moments of sexism? Or does she expose the bad feelings that get hidden, displaced, or negated under public signs of joy?
quote.author: Sara Ahmed

shame.text: Shame is one of the most tormenting feelings: you want to disappear, to hide your face. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed shows that shame is always bound up with others. We feel ashamed before someone’s gaze — real or imagined — and we are ashamed because we have fallen short of an ideal that matters to us and to those whose love we want to keep. Shame, for Ahmed, turns the self against itself: the gaze turns inward, the body seems to shrink. But there is consolation in this description too: shame shows how deeply you value your connection with people and their recognition. You can ask yourself whose ideal this is and whether it is really yours. Sometimes shame simply reports that you have ended up outside someone else’s norm — not that you are a bad person.
shame.practice: Before whose eyes — even imagined ones — are you ashamed right now? Write down what someone who looks at you with kindness would say to you.

guilt.text: Guilt is a painful but very human feeling: it says that you care how your actions have affected others. Affect theory writes little about guilt directly, but from Sara Ahmed’s point of view something important can be said. Analyzing public apologies and “national shame,” Ahmed notices a trap: admitting guilt sometimes becomes a way of feeling good about ourselves again, and attention returns to the one who is guilty rather than to the one who was harmed. Hence a gentle conclusion: endlessly punishing yourself is not the same as repairing a relationship. Guilt “sticks” and can spread far beyond the act itself. It can be brought back to its real size: what exactly happened, whom it affected, and what is actually possible to do now.
guilt.practice: Describe in two sentences what exactly happened — without judging yourself. Is there one small step directed toward the other person rather than toward punishing yourself?

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant to admit, but it is very common and tells us a lot about ourselves. Ahmed hardly writes about envy directly, but her idea of “happy objects” clarifies a great deal here. In The Promise of Happiness she shows that culture tells us in advance which things are supposed to make us happy: a certain career, marriage, a house, a body. These objects carry a promise, and we reach for them without even choosing. And in “affective economies,” for Ahmed, feelings accumulate value as they circulate: the more often the image of a “happy life” flashes before our eyes, the stronger its pull. From this point of view, one could say that your envy is not a vice but a trace of these promises. You can examine it: what do you actually want, and what has been promised to you from outside?
envy.practice: Write down what you envy right now, and next to it what promise you think is hidden in this “object.” Does it sound like your own desire?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be very heavy — especially when it seems there is “no reason” for them. In The Promise of Happiness, Sara Ahmed recalls “the problem that has no name” described by Betty Friedan: women in the mid-20th century lived the life that was considered happy — home, family, prosperity — and felt a strange emptiness inside. Ahmed sees this not as a personal defect but as a sign that the promise of happiness invested in the “right” life had not worked. From this point of view, one could say that your emptiness can be an honest response to a life running on someone else’s script. In Massumi’s spirit, one can add: even in an apparent lull, the body keeps sensing — intensity doesn’t disappear completely, it just hasn’t found words yet. Emptiness is not the end of feeling but a pause in it.
emptiness.practice: Notice one tiny sensation in your body right now — the warmth of your palms, the ground under your feet. Simply note that it is there.

confusion.text: Confusion is frightening: the ground seems to slip from under your feet, and it’s unclear where to go. In Queer Phenomenology, Sara Ahmed writes about exactly such moments and calls them disorientation. When the familiar lines along which life moves suddenly stop holding, the body loses its footing, and for a while the world seems “askew.” Ahmed is in no hurry to regard this as only a misfortune: disorientation shows that our directions were not natural — they were formed by repetition, habits, other people’s expectations. In such moments it becomes visible that you could turn another way. That doesn’t make confusion pleasant. But it can be lived as a transitional state in which new directions open up, rather than as proof that you have “lost your way.”
confusion.practice: Ask yourself: which of the familiar “lines” — expectations, plans, routes — has stopped holding right now? And what has become visible because of it?

fatigue.text: Fatigue and burnout are not laziness or weakness of character. In Living a Feminist Life, Sara Ahmed writes about how wearing it is to keep coming up against “brick walls” — obstacles visible only to those who run into them. Pressure builds up unnoticed, and one day something “snaps”: it seems the person broke down suddenly, although in fact it is the result of long strain. Ahmed also rethinks self-care, drawing on the poet Audre Lorde: for those whom the world depletes, self-care is not a whim but a way to survive and keep going. From this point of view, your tiredness is a meaningful response to the load. Rest here is not a reward for results but a condition for remaining yourself.
fatigue.practice: Think of one “wall” you have been running into lately. What one small thing could support you today — not for the sake of productivity, but for your own sake?

quote.text: Caring for myself is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation, and that is an act of political warfare.
quote.author: Audre Lorde

boredom.text: Boredom seems like a small feeling, but it can be truly oppressive: time drags, everything looks flat. Affect theory writes little about boredom directly, but from Massumi’s point of view the following can be said. Affect, following Spinoza and Deleuze, is the capacity to affect and to be affected. Boredom resembles a state in which this capacity has temporarily narrowed: the world keeps touching us, but the touches don’t get through. Massumi speaks of “microshocks” — tiny shifts of attention that make up every moment of perception. They are there now too: a change in the light, a sound, your own breathing. Boredom in this light is not the emptiness of the world but a muffling of contact with it. It doesn’t have to be drowned out with new stimuli; sometimes it is enough to notice, a little more slowly, what is already happening.
boredom.practice: For one minute, become a “collector of microshocks”: note the three smallest changes around you — a sound, a movement, a shift in the light.

joy.text: Joy does not need to be earned or justified — it happens, and that is wonderful. For Massumi, heir to Spinoza, affect has to do with whether our capacity to act and feel increases or decreases; joy is the moment when this capacity expands and the body seems to grow larger. Sara Ahmed, while criticizing the “duty to be happy,” is not at all against joy. She reminds us that the English word happiness comes from hap — “chance,” “luck”: happiness was originally connected with what simply befalls us, not with living rightly according to plan. Ahmed suggests giving happiness back this element of chance. So your joy doesn’t have to be built into a grand story of success. You can simply let it be — like an unexpected gift of the moment.
joy.practice: What exactly “happened” to you and brought joy? Describe it in one sentence, as a small event.

love.text: Love and tenderness are feelings that make us both stronger and more vulnerable. If, following Massumi, we understand affect as the capacity to affect and be affected, then love is one of the forms in which this capacity flourishes: another person begins to change your rhythm, your breathing, your thoughts. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed stresses that love is not only a private feeling: it orients us, turns us toward someone, and out of it a “we” is formed. Ahmed soberly notes that this “we” is sometimes built by excluding others. But the capacity to love itself is how the world becomes shared. You can accept your tenderness not as weakness but as a sign of openness: your boundaries are mobile and alive.
love.practice: Notice how love changes you bodily — your posture, your voice, your pace. Describe it in a word or two.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling in which we notice that someone or something has supported us. From Ahmed’s point of view, one could say that gratitude, like other emotions, circulates: it passes from person to person, connects, makes bonds visible. But Ahmed also teaches attentiveness: in The Promise of Happiness she shows how certain people — migrants, for example — are expected to have the “right” feelings: to be happy and content with what they have been given. Gratitude that is demanded stops being gratitude and becomes a debt. So it is worth distinguishing: is your gratitude alive and free — or do you feel obliged to feel it? Real gratitude does not cancel the right to see what was wrong as well. It can live alongside other feelings without crowding them out.
gratitude.practice: Name one thing you are grateful for without any effort — and one thing you are more or less expected to be grateful for.

hope.text: Hope is a quiet strength that helps us keep going, and it is worth protecting. In his reflections on hope, Brian Massumi proposes separating it from the expectation of success. If you hope only for a big goal or a guaranteed result, hope becomes fragile: any failure brings it down. Massumi looks for hope in the present — in what he calls a “margin of maneuverability”: in every situation, even a tight one, there is a small space where the next step can be taken slightly differently. Hope in this sense is neither a forecast nor optimism but a feeling of openness, a sense that the situation is not yet finished. This is a relief: you don’t have to believe that everything will definitely be fine in order to feel that something is possible right now.
hope.practice: Where in your current situation is there at least a small “margin of maneuverability”? Write down one next step that could be taken slightly differently.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is sweet and aching at once, and there is nothing naive about it. Sara Ahmed writes that emotions “stick” to objects: a smell, a melody, an old photograph become “sticky” with the feelings associated with them and, years later, bring them back whole. In Massumi’s spirit one can add that this memory lives in the body before it lives in words: the body recognizes a familiar intonation faster than we can recall where it comes from. Ahmed also notes that nostalgia can be collective — for the “good old days,” which were not good for everyone. But personal nostalgia above all shows what has stuck to you and what shaped you. You can accept it as a gentle touch of the past, without demanding that the past return.
nostalgia.practice: What smell, sound or object “sticks” most strongly to your past? Stay with this image for a minute and notice what it awakens in you.

quote.text: Affect is what sticks, or what sustains or preserves the connection between ideas, values, and objects.
quote.author: Sara Ahmed

craving.text: A sharp craving — for a cigarette, a drink, your phone — can hit so hard that it feels as if the decision has already been made for you. This is hard, and there is nothing shameful in it. Massumi, drawing on neurophysiological experiments, writes about the “missing half-second”: the body begins a movement slightly before consciousness has time to “decide” it. Affect is always a little ahead of thought. Sara Ahmed adds in Queer Phenomenology that our actions are largely shaped by what is “within reach” — what the body is used to reaching for. From this point of view, a craving is not a verdict on your character but a bodily impulse laid down by repetition. But an impulse is not yet an act. Between the wave and the action you can create a tiny gap, and by changing what is within reach you can change the very direction of movement. The wave rises and falls.
craving.practice: Move the object of the craving at least a couple of meters away — into another room, into a drawer. Notice how the wave changes when it isn’t within reach.

addiction.text: When life has been built around one thing for years, getting out of the circle is very hard, and it is not a moral weakness. In What’s the Use? (2019), Sara Ahmed writes about paths: the more often a path is walked, the more visible and easier it becomes, and the more readily people walk it again. A path no one walks becomes overgrown. She applies this idea to habits and institutions: use lays down direction. From the standpoint of affect theory, one could say that addiction is a very well-trodden path along which the body and feelings go almost by themselves. This explains why leaving it is so hard — and lifts some of the shame. But Ahmed also talks about “desire lines”: paths people tread themselves, bypassing the official routes. A new path is laid down gradually — step by step, and often together with others.
addiction.practice: Name one small “new path” — a walk, a call, a short task — that you could walk today. If you like, you can walk it together with someone who understands, for example in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after — heaviness in the body, anxiety, shame and gaps in memory — is a very uncomfortable state, and it does not make you a bad person. Massumi emphasizes that the body registers more than the mind has time to grasp: intensities leave a trace even when they have no words. That is why in the morning anxiety can be stronger than the “facts” warrant — the body has not yet recovered. Sara Ahmed writes that feelings “stick” to objects: a vague shame easily sticks to any scrap of memory and inflates it. From this point of view, one could say that part of the morning dread is not knowledge about last night but affect looking for something to stick to. You can notice it without taking it on faith. First, take care of your body. Later, when it is calmer, your view of last night will be calmer too.
hangover.practice: Notice where in your body anxiety and shame are sitting right now. Tell yourself: “This is a state of the body, not a final verdict” — and drink some water.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria, when everything seems possible, is a vivid experience, and you can enjoy it. Massumi, following Spinoza, describes affect as an increase or decrease in the capacity to act. Euphoria is a moment of sharp increase: the body seems to grow larger, and the world opens up with possibilities. Massumi calls this sensation “virtual” — not unreal, but a field of the possible that for a moment becomes tangible. Not all possibilities will be realized, but that doesn’t make the feeling false: you really did feel how much wider your life could be. From this point of view, euphoria need neither be held on to nor immediately turned into decisions. You can simply live it and remember it as knowledge that openness is possible. When the high subsides, that knowledge will stay with you.
euphoria.practice: Write in one sentence what possibility feels open to you right now. Not as a plan, but as a memory that you felt it.

crash.text: A sharp comedown after a high — a celebration, a success, a vivid evening — can be bitter: as if everything has faded. In The Promise of Happiness, Sara Ahmed writes about “happy objects” — holidays, achievements, events that promise joy in advance. When the event is over, what remains is not only tiredness but also the gap between the promise and what is left afterward. Massumi adds that intensity by its nature does not last long: it flares up and dissipates, and the body returns to its usual rhythm. From this point of view, one could say that the “comedown” is neither proof that the joy was fake nor a sign that you are broken. It is the normal movement of an affect that has ebbed. The dip doesn’t need to be urgently filled with a new high. You can let your body rest from the intensity.
crash.practice: Name one small, quiet thing that will support your body today: sleep, food, a warm shower. Do it without guilt.

panic.text: A panic attack is genuinely frightening: your heart pounds, your breath catches, it seems something irreversible is about to happen. Massumi emphasizes that affect happens in the body before thought: heart, breath and muscles react a split second before the word “fear” appears. He writes about how a threat that has not yet happened can feel completely real in the body. From this point of view, one could say that panic is a wave of intensity that seizes the body faster than the mind can name it. That is why what helps is not arguing with your thoughts but turning to the body — in its own language. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. While it lasts, the body can be supported with breath and grounding, the way you would support a friend.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and make your exhale longer than your inhale. Name out loud three things you see, two you hear, and one you feel on your skin.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is it all for,” the sense of finitude and of the abyss — is a heavy experience, and many people know it. Sara Ahmed writes that anxiety, unlike fear, is not attached to a single object: it slides from one thing to another, sticking now to the future, now to death, now to meaninglessness. Dread may be anxiety in its widest form — stuck to everything at once. Massumi, for his part, says that every moment holds an excess — life is more than what we manage to live and name in it. From this point of view, one could say that the abyss you feel is precisely this excess, which does not fit into an answer. It can be frightening, but it also means that life is not exhausted and that something in it always remains open.
dread.practice: Notice what your dread has “stuck” to right now. Then find one sensation that is happening right now — warmth, a sound, your breath — and stay with it for a minute.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you are not where you should be is painful and very widespread. Sara Ahmed reminds us that the English word happiness comes from hap — “chance,” “what happens.” But culture has turned happiness into a route: the right places, the right parties, the right life. Ahmed calls such routes “happiness scripts” and shows how they make those who don’t follow them feel “out of place.” From this point of view, one could say that the fear of missing out is not your failure but an effect of a script that promises happiness happens somewhere out there. But if you give happiness back its “hap,” it turns out it can happen anywhere — including where you are now.
fomo.practice: Notice one small thing that “happened” to you today — a meeting, a taste, the light. It wasn’t part of any script.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and three-in-the-morning thoughts are exhausting, and in the dark everything seems more hopeless. Sara Ahmed writes that anxiety is “sticky”: it jumps from object to object, sticking now to work, now to health, now to relationships. At night, without the day’s tasks, this movement is especially noticeable — anxiety circles round and round, finding ever new occasions. Massumi emphasizes that affect lives in the body: even when thoughts seem endless, this is above all the state of an aroused organism. From this point of view, one could say that night thoughts are not an insight about life but anxiety looking for something to stick to. It doesn’t need to be resolved with logic at three in the morning. You can turn to the body — breath, warmth, heaviness — and let it slowly calm down.
sleepless.practice: Notice what the anxiety is sticking to now and say inwardly: “There it is again.” Then slowly feel the heaviness of your arms and legs on the bed.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only trust in a person but the sense that the world is something you can lean on. In On Being Included (2012), Sara Ahmed introduced the concept of “non-performatives” — statements that promise to do something but in fact do not do it: “we support you,” “you can count on us.” Ahmed wrote about such promises made by organizations, but from her point of view one can say the same about personal relationships: betrayal is a promise that was spoken and not kept. The pain of it is especially sharp because you oriented yourself by those words and built your life on them. Your pain is not naivety but evidence that you trusted. And that trust was not a mistake but a capacity worth keeping for those who deserve it.
betrayal.practice: Write down which words or promises you relied on. Then write down one action by a person in your life that matched their words.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a burning and very human feeling: the fear of losing someone dear. Massumi emphasizes that affect arrives in the body before we can think it over: a pang of jealousy can happen in a fraction of a second — from a look, a word, a notification. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed shows how love can turn into fear and hostility when it seems that a beloved object is threatened by a third party. The feeling starts to “stick” to that figure. From the standpoint of affect theory, one could say that jealousy is neither proof of infidelity nor a sign that you are rotten, but love mixed with the fear of loss. If you notice how quickly and bodily it arises, you can give yourself a pause before acting: the wave does not have to become a deed.
jealousy.practice: When a pang of jealousy comes, place your hand where you feel it and take three slow breaths before doing anything.

resentment.text: A long-held grievance that you carry for years is heavy, and it cannot be let go on command. In Complaint! (2021), Sara Ahmed studied what happens to complaints that are not heard. She shows that they do not disappear but get “stuck” — in bodies, in files, in the corridors of institutions. People keep carrying them for years because there was nowhere to take them. From Ahmed’s point of view, one could say that resentment is often a complaint that found no listener. Its long life is not your pettiness but a sign that it was never taken seriously. Ahmed also speaks of a “feminist ear” — the capacity to hear what usually goes unheard. Sometimes resentment eases when someone finally hears it — even if that someone is you.
resentment.practice: Write your grievance down as a complaint: what happened, what was violated, what you couldn’t say at the time. Read it aloud to yourself, like a friend who believes you.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts literally, with the whole body, and it takes time. Sara Ahmed writes that love is an orientation: we turn toward a person and build our days, paths and habits around them. When a relationship ends, the direction you were turned toward disappears, and for a while the world loses its shape. Besides, feelings “stick” to things: a song, a café, a street remain soaked in a shared past and unexpectedly wound you. From this point of view, one could say that your pain is not weakness but a reflection of how strongly you were oriented toward this person. Ahmed also writes about “reorientation”: gradually the body learns to turn toward new things. This does not happen quickly, and there is no need to rush yourself.
heartbreak.practice: Notice one thing that is “sticking” to the past right now and hurts. You don’t need to get rid of it — just name it and let it be for now.

impostor.text: The fear that you are about to be exposed is agonizing, and it is familiar to many very capable people. Sara Ahmed, following the sociologist Nirmal Puwar, writes about “space invaders” — people who end up in places not originally designed for them: because of gender, background, class, age. Such people often feel that their presence is in question, even when they are doing everything well. From Ahmed’s point of view, one could say that feeling like an impostor is often not knowledge of your incompetence but a sense of not matching the “norm” of a space that was set before you arrived. This is not your fault. Ahmed shows that your very presence in such places already changes them — and makes them a little more open to others.
impostor.practice: Write down how you are “unlike” the typical person in your environment. Then write what, thanks to this difference, you see or can do differently.

self_hatred.text: When the inner critic says you are bad and worthless, it hurts a great deal — and its verdict is not the truth about you. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed shows that hate is not born in one person: it circulates in society, is passed from some to others and “sticks” to certain bodies and figures. From this point of view, one could say that self-hatred is often not your own discovery about yourself but internalized disdain that was once directed at you, or at people like you, and then stuck from within. Ahmed emphasizes that what has stuck can be noticed and gradually separated. The critic’s voice sounds like yours, but its words have often come from somewhere else. You don’t have to keep passing them on.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one of the inner critic’s phrases and ask: where did I first hear something like this? Is this voice really mine?

helplessness.text: Powerlessness to change anything is hard to bear, especially when you are trying very hard. Massumi, drawing on Spinoza, defines affect as the capacity to affect and to be affected. This matters: even when you can do almost nothing, your capacity to be affected is not a weakness — it too is a form of participation in the world. In Living a Feminist Life, Sara Ahmed offers a “survival kit” for those who come up against insurmountable walls: books, things that sustain you, time, humor, your feelings, your body, and other people who understand. From this point of view, one could say that when you can’t change everything, you can gather what helps you hold on. This is not surrender but a way of keeping yourself for the moment when change becomes possible.
helplessness.practice: Assemble your own small “survival kit”: write down three things, people or activities that help you hold on when little depends on you.

procrastination.text: When you can’t get started even though you really need to, it’s easy to start berating yourself. Massumi writes that every action begins not with a decision but with a barely noticeable bodily movement — an “incipient tendency” that has not yet taken shape as an act. Sara Ahmed adds in Queer Phenomenology that we more easily do what is within reach and what we are already turned toward. From this point of view, one could say that procrastination is not laziness but a situation in which the task is “out of reach”: too big, frightening, or unconnected with where your body is turned. Instead of pressuring yourself, you can bring the task closer — lay out the materials, open the file — and let a tiny movement become a beginning.
procrastination.practice: Make the task “reachable”: put the thing you need in front of you or open the file. Nothing more is required — just stay near it for a minute.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — after emigration or a move — can go very deep: as if the world around you doesn’t recognize you, and the old world is gone. Sara Ahmed and colleagues edited the collection Uprootings/Regroundings (2003) on migration and home, and in Strange Encounters (2000) she wrote about how we come to be perceived as “strangers.” She shows that home is not only a place but also habits, smells, rhythms, the bodies around you: what you were oriented toward. In a new place this orientation is lost, and the body literally doesn’t know which way to turn. From Ahmed’s point of view, one could say that your disorientation is a normal response to losing a familiar orientation. Home is not simply lost; it is also created anew — through new habits, connections, and people who also know what it’s like to be “not from here.”
uprooted.practice: Choose one small habit from your former life — a dish, a song, a walk at a certain time — and repeat it in your new place this week.

overload.text: Overload from the endless feed, notifications and news is exhausting, and it is not your inability to “cope.” In his famous essay “The Autonomy of Affect,” Massumi showed that media act on us primarily through intensity rather than content: tone, rhythm and image touch the body before we grasp the meaning. So the feed acts on the nervous system as a stream of small blows, even when it communicates nothing important. From this point of view, one could say that feed fatigue is not a whim but the reaction of a body taking on too much intensity at once. It is not obliged to withstand an endless stream. Sometimes the wisest thing is to remove the source for a while and let the nervous system return to its own rhythm.
overload.practice: Put your phone aside for ten minutes and notice what happens in your body: your breathing, your shoulders, your gaze. Mark the moment when it became even a little quieter.

unreality.text: The feeling that the world, or you yourself, are somehow not quite real can be frightening and disorienting. In Queer Phenomenology, Sara Ahmed describes moments of disorientation when the world seems to “slip” and appears at a strange angle: the familiar suddenly stops being familiar. Massumi shows that consciousness always lags slightly behind the body — by that very “half-second.” Usually we don’t notice this gap, but sometimes it seems to stretch, and life feels as if it is happening behind glass. From this point of view, one could say that the feeling of unreality is an experience of a particular position between body and world, not proof that the world has vanished. The body goes on living and sensing. The gentle way back is through the simplest sensations it responds to.
unreality.practice: Take something with a pronounced texture or temperature in your hands — a mug, a stone, cold water — and describe to yourself what your fingers feel.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed writes about wonder as a special emotion: the world suddenly appears as if you were seeing it for the first time, and the familiar stops being taken for granted. For her, wonder is also a way of seeing that the world could have been otherwise and at some point became what it is. Massumi would describe awe as an intensity that exceeds any capacity to name it: the body is seized before words appear. From this point of view, awe is not something to explain or immediately photograph. It is a moment when the capacity to be affected expands to its limit. You can simply live it and let it change you.
awe.practice: Stay with whatever filled you with awe for one more minute without words. Then ask: what did I just see as if for the first time?

relief.text: Relief is a warm feeling when tension finally lets go, and it is worth savoring. Sara Ahmed writes about comfort as a fit between body and space: when the body can “sink” into a chair, a place, a situation, it doesn’t need to hold itself tense all the time. Relief is the moment when the body can sink like that again after a long period of holding itself together. Massumi would emphasize that this is above all a bodily event: muscles, breath and heart change rhythm before we say “thank God.” From this point of view, one could say that relief is worth not only realizing but living through the body, letting it relax completely. It shows how much strength went into the tension — and reminds you that the body knows how to let go.
relief.practice: Let your body “sink” into what supports it — a chair, a bed, the floor. Notice which muscles have let go, and stay like this for a minute.

calm.text: Calm and peace are infrequent guests, and it is good to cherish them. In Queer Phenomenology, Sara Ahmed reflects on the “background” — things that recede so that we can attend to other things: the table, the chair, the familiar room. Usually the background goes unnoticed until something disturbs it. From this point of view, one could say that calm is a state in which the background can remain background, nothing demands urgent attention and the world feels reliable. Massumi would call it a time when intensity is quiet and even and the body is not mobilized. Calm doesn’t have to turn into productivity. You can simply be in it and notice what usually slips away: the quiet of the room, the light, your own breath.
calm.practice: Notice one thing from the “background” around you — a wall, the light, a sound outside the window — and stay with it for a minute, doing nothing else.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful feeling, when something new seems to be asking to come out on its own. In Semblance and Event (2011), Massumi writes about “thinking-feeling”: a moment when thought and sensation are not yet separated and something is only beginning to take shape. It is not a plan but an incipient tendency full of possibility. Sara Ahmed speaks of “desire lines” — paths that people tread themselves, bypassing the paved routes. From this point of view, one could say that inspiration is the moment when you sense such a new path without yet knowing where it leads. It doesn’t need to be turned into a result right away. Let yourself walk a few steps along it — just to feel how the world changes when you walk differently.
inspiration.practice: Write the idea down the way it came — without structuring or judging it. Notice where in your body you feel this inspiration.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — a prick of pleasure at someone else’s failure — is a feeling people hide even from themselves. Affect theory invites us to look at such states without moralizing. In Ugly Feelings (2005), Sianne Ngai explores “minor,” unflattering emotions — envy, irritation, anxiety. In her view, they offer neither catharsis nor a sense of being in the right, and they often arise where a person has little opportunity to act: movement seems blocked. From this point of view, one could say that schadenfreude is also like an “ugly feeling”: a tiny compensation for the sense that you yourself are stuck while someone else’s success weighs on you. This feeling does not define you. Rather, it points to a place where you lack movement. If you notice it without shame, you can ask: what do I want for myself?
schadenfreude.practice: Recall a moment of schadenfreude and write: where in my life do I feel stuck right now? One sentence is enough.

contempt.text: Contempt is hard to admit: there is coldness and superiority in it. But affect theory helps us see its bodily nature. The psychologist Silvan Tomkins, whose ideas affect theory draws on, singled out among the basic affects a special reaction to bad smells (he called it “dissmell”): we wrinkle our nose and pull back, not letting something come closer. Contempt, for Tomkins, is related to this gesture: it is a way of keeping another at a distance. Sara Ahmed adds that such feelings draw boundaries between “us” and “them.” From this point of view, your contempt is above all a signal: something in this person feels like a threat to your order, your values or your peace. There is no need to reproach yourself for it. You can ask: what am I protecting myself from by pulling away — and do I need that distance?
contempt.practice: Notice what contempt looks like in your body: pressed lips, a raised chin, an averted gaze? Gently relax your face and see what remains of the feeling.

disgust.text: Disgust is a very bodily feeling: you want to recoil from a person, a situation, sometimes from yourself. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed devotes a whole chapter to disgust and notes a paradox: disgust presupposes closeness. We are disgusted by what has already come too close, touched us, as if it had “stuck.” In pushing it away, we also draw a boundary: “this is not me.” Ahmed stresses that these boundaries are not natural: culture teaches us what to consider disgusting, and such judgments often “stick” to whole groups of people. From this point of view, disgust is the work of a boundary, not an objective truth about what provokes it. This matters especially when disgust is directed at yourself: it may be an echo of other people’s judgments. You can question it rather than take it on faith.
disgust.practice: Name what disgusts you and ask yourself: how did I learn that this is “disgusting”? Think about whose voice that might have been.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge rises like a wave after an injury, and that is understandable: you were hurt. Brian Massumi distinguishes affect from emotion. Affect is bodily intensity, a surge that arises before thought; emotion is what it takes shape as once it gets a name and a plot. Intensity, for Massumi, is always richer than any form: it holds many possible continuations, and only one of them becomes action. From this point of view, the thirst for revenge is one of the plots into which your strength might be cast, but far from the only one. The same energy can become a resolve to protect yourself, to name an injustice, to draw a boundary. There is no need to deny the rage. You can give it time and notice what other paths it opens — without harming anyone.
revenge.practice: Feel where in your body this rage lives, and take a few slow exhales. Then write down three different actions this energy could turn into — none of which may harm anyone.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at the people closest to you — a partner, parents, children — is one of the most shameful feelings, although it is one of the most ordinary. In The Promise of Happiness, Sara Ahmed shows that the family is one of the main “happy objects” of our culture: warmth, harmony and joy are expected of it in advance. So anger within a family feels like breaking the rules, and whoever feels it seems like the destroyer of the shared harmony. Ahmed notes that behind this picture there is often an unequal burden: someone is constantly giving way, caring, keeping quiet so that everyone can feel “fine.” From this point of view, your anger may be reporting a real problem — exhaustion, an unfair distribution of care, unspoken hurts. This is no reason to lash out at your loved ones. But it is no reason to consider yourself a monster either: anger is a signal worth hearing.
anger_at_loved.practice: Write down one thing you do in your family “so that everyone feels fine” that wears you out. You don’t need to change anything right away — just name it.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is a very common combination, although it is rarely spoken of aloud. Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, one of the founders of affect theory, drew here on the psychoanalyst Melanie Klein. Klein described how an infant first divides the world into “good” and “bad,” and later — in the so-called “depressive position” — learns to see that the one it loves and the one who hurts it are the same person. Sedgwick linked this position to “reparativeness,” the capacity to repair: to assemble a whole out of contradictory parts. From this point of view, your ambivalence is not a breakdown of love but a sign of a mature view. You don’t have to choose one feeling. You can hold both, and that holding is itself already the work of repair.
ambivalence.practice: Draw a circle and write inside it both what you love in this person and what you find hard to bear. Look: it is one and the same person — and that is okay.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a seriously ill loved one is often frightening: how can I feel lightness if I love? For such situations Sara Ahmed offers the expression “affect alien.” That is what she calls a person who feels something other than what they are “supposed” to: who is sad at a celebration or cannot grieve in the way others expect. Culture hands out scripts of correct feelings, and deviating from them feels like guilt. But, for Ahmed, such mismatches are common and honestly tell us a lot about our lives. From this point of view, your relief is not a betrayal of love but the body’s response to the end of a long strain. Love and relief do not cancel each other out. You can grieve and at the same time feel that it has become easier to breathe.
guilty_relief.practice: Take a few calm breaths and say to yourself: “I feel lighter — and I still love.” Notice how your body responds to these words.

indifference.text: Sometimes, where something “should” move you, there is emptiness. This is frightening: do I really not care? In Ugly Feelings, Sianne Ngai proposes the concept of “stuplimity” — from “stupor” and “the sublime.” With it she describes a state in which shock and boredom mix: when impressions are too many and they keep repeating, sensitivity seems to go dull. Ngai stresses that this is not an absence of feeling but a particular form of it — a response to being overfull. From this point of view, your indifference may be not coldness but protection: the psyche muffles the signal because there is too much of it. Massumi would add that affect keeps acting in the body even when it hasn’t taken shape as an emotion. The feeling may return later, in quiet. There is no need to squeeze it out of yourself.
indifference.practice: Put away all sources of news and feeds for half an hour. Then listen to your body: has anything changed — even tiredness, even warmth?

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and leave — a job, a city, a familiar role — can be sudden and strong. This is about the wish to change your circumstances, not to leave life. In Queer Phenomenology, Sara Ahmed writes about the lines along which we move: life often follows well-trodden paths, and the more people have walked them, the more natural they seem. Ahmed recalls the image of “desire lines” — paths people wear across a lawn, bypassing the laid-out routes. From this point of view, the wish to escape is a sign that your path may not run where the road has been laid. It is neither a whim nor weakness. You don’t have to take off immediately. But it is worth noticing where your own path is pulling — and taking at least a small step along it.
escape.practice: Write down where you would turn if you were walking “across the lawn” rather than along the path. What is the smallest step in that direction that’s possible this week?

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to the “wrong” or an unavailable person is often embarrassing and confusing. Affect theory passes no moral verdicts on it. In Queer Phenomenology, Sara Ahmed writes that desire is an orientation: we turn toward some objects and away from others. But what ends up “within reach” is largely set in advance — by habits, norms, the paths we have walked. That is why desire directed “the wrong way” feels like a malfunction. Ahmed, however, shows that deviations from straight lines are part of how living bodies move through the world. From this point of view, one could say that such attraction speaks of a living turn in you — toward something you are lacking right now. You don’t need to decide right away what to do with it. You can ask yourself what exactly you have turned toward.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down, in one word, what quality or sensation draws you to this person. Where else in your life is there at least a trace of this quality?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment often lives in the body: your cheeks burn, your throat goes dry, your heart pounds before you have thought anything. In the essay “The Autonomy of Affect,” Brian Massumi describes this feature: the body reacts before consciousness — about half a second passes between a surge of intensity and our awareness of it. Massumi calls affect “autonomous”: it does not obey the will directly. This explains why being told to “just don’t worry” doesn’t work. From this point of view, your reaction is not foolishness or weakness of character but the fast work of a body responding to the presence of others. There is no need to be ashamed of it. You can let the wave pass and notice: the nervousness is there, but it is not all that is in me. Others most likely see it much less than you think.
social_anxiety.practice: In a moment of nervousness, feel your feet on the floor and make your exhale longer than your inhale. Tell yourself: “My body got there before me — that’s normal.”

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is exhausting: you don’t know what will happen, and you long for at least some clarity. The anthropologist Kathleen Stewart, close to affect theory, describes everyday life in Ordinary Affects (2007) as a flow in which something is always emerging, shifting, beginning. In her view, ordinary life consists not of clear plans but of many small events that are felt by the body before they come together into a story. Stewart urges us to notice these small shifts, not just wait for a big answer. From this point of view, uncertainty is not only an anxious void but also a living “something is happening,” in which good things are possible too. This doesn’t require you to “reframe your anxiety positively.” But you can shift your attention from the vast unknown to the small thing that is already happening now.
uncertainty.practice: Write down three small events of today — a sound, a conversation, a change in the weather. This too is the future, already happening.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — drags on painfully: all your attention is turned toward a moment that has not yet arrived. In the interviews collected in Politics of Affect (2015), Brian Massumi speaks about hope in a particular way. For him, hope is not confidence in a good outcome but a sense of openness present in every moment: any “now” contains more possibilities than we notice. When we are wholly directed toward a future answer, the present shrinks to an empty gap. From this point of view, one could say that waiting is easier if you bring your attention back to the present — not to distract yourself but to see that life is going on now too. The result will come when it comes. And this moment is already here.
waiting.practice: Set a timer for two minutes and simply notice what is happening around you: sounds, light, sensations in your body. There is no answer yet — but you do have these two minutes.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn’t do often goes round in circles: “if only I had…” In the essay “Paranoid Reading and Reparative Reading,” Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick distinguishes two positions. The “paranoid” one strives to foresee everything and protect itself in advance from bad surprises; it endlessly double-checks what went wrong. The “reparative” one allows itself to hope: it acknowledges that the future may differ from the present — and therefore that the past could have turned out differently too. It sounds paradoxical, but it is freeing: back then you acted in concrete circumstances, not according to an inevitable law. From this point of view, regret doesn’t have to become a self-trial. It can be turned into care — for what can still be repaired, and for the version of yourself that went through all this.
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and then one small “reparative” action that is possible now: a word, a letter, care for yourself or for someone else.

quote.text: …it is also possible for her to entertain such profoundly painful, profoundly relieving, ethically crucial possibilities as that the past, in turn, could have happened differently from the way it actually did.
quote.author: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick
quote.source: “Paranoid Reading and Reparative Reading,” in Touching Feeling (2003)

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is a feeling with a face, a voice, a smell. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed speaks about emotions through the word “impression.” It has two senses: an opinion about something, and a trace, an imprint on a surface. Other people, for Ahmed, literally leave impressions on us: their presence shapes our habits, gestures, the way we move through the world. When the person is not near, the impression remains — and aches, like a place where something is missing. From this point of view, your longing is neither weakness nor dependence but evidence of how deeply you were touched. The impression doesn’t need to be erased. Over time it can become not a wound but a part of you that you carry with care.
longing.practice: Notice one habit, gesture or turn of phrase of yours that came from this person. Let yourself smile at this trace, even if it is sad.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — for those who suffer from wars, violence, injustice — can be almost physical, especially when the news keeps pouring in. In the chapter on pain in The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed writes that it is impossible to feel another’s pain exactly as they feel it. But for Ahmed this does not imply indifference: ethics consists in allowing ourselves to be affected by what we cannot fully know. Ahmed also warns of something else: compassion should not turn someone else’s pain into a story about ourselves. From this point of view, your pain is a sign of openness to the world, and it is valuable. But you don’t have to carry it alone and without a break. You can let yourself feel — and look for concrete ways, within your means, to stand by those who are struggling.
world_pain.practice: Place your hand on your chest and say: “I cannot know this pain fully, but I do not turn it away.” Then choose one small, concrete act of support.

rejection.text: Rejection — when you weren’t accepted into a circle, weren’t chosen, were turned away from — wounds deeply. In Strange Encounters (2000), Sara Ahmed writes about the figure of the “stranger.” The stranger, in her view, is not someone we don’t know but someone we recognize as “out of place.” The boundary between “us” and “strangers” is created by the group itself, by its habits and expectations, not by the qualities of the person rejected. From this point of view, rejection says more about how that circle is arranged than about your worth. The pain doesn’t disappear because of this, and it shouldn’t be minimized: we all need to belong. But you don’t have to accept someone else’s boundary as a verdict on yourself — and you can look for places where you are not a “stranger” but one of their own.
rejection.practice: Recall a place or a group where you feel “in place.” What is different there? Write down one detail.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is one of the most ancient: without others, a human being does not survive. Brian Massumi stresses that affect is always about relationships. In an interview from Politics of Affect, he describes affect as our participation in processes larger than ourselves, and says that strong feelings sharpen our sense of being woven into life, of belonging to other people and places. We exist not as closed units but as knots in a field of connections. That is why the threat of losing someone close is perceived by the body as a threat to our very footing, even if the mind understands that you will cope. From this point of view, your fear is not an exaggeration but a sensitivity to how much connections mean to you. But the field of relationships is always wider than one person. You can notice the other threads that hold you too — even thin ones.
abandonment.practice: Write down five connections that hold you, besides the one you are afraid of losing: people, places, activities, even animals or habits.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love hurts in a particular way: the feeling is real, and there is no answer. In The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Sara Ahmed, drawing on Freud, notes that in love we often love not only the other person but also a certain ideal — an image of who we could become beside them, of what our world could be. So unrequitedness wounds twice over: there is no answer from the person, and this ideal image of ourselves seems to collapse. From this point of view, one could say that part of your pain is about a lost future you had already imagined. This is not naivety: this is how love works. That image may also say something about what you want for yourself. You can keep it and look for other paths toward it — not only through this person.
unrequited.practice: Write down how you saw yourself beside this person. Choose one trait from this image that you can develop without them.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is a feeling that makes you want to hide, lower your eyes, leave the room. Silvan Tomkins, whose ideas Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick rediscovered for the humanities, combined shame and humiliation into a single affect — “shame-humiliation.” For Tomkins, it arises not when we don’t care but when interest or joy is interrupted without being extinguished: we were reaching toward people, toward recognition, and the connection was suddenly broken. Lowered eyes and a burning face are the bodily trace of this rupture. From this point of view, your humiliation speaks not of your worthlessness but of how much connection with people matters to you. Sedgwick emphasized that shame is deeply social and contagious: it often belongs more to the situation than to you. You can remind yourself: I needed contact, and there is nothing shameful in that.
humiliation.practice: Place your palm on your face or your chest, as if comforting someone dear to you. Tell yourself: “I was reaching out to people. That is not shameful.”

body_shame.text: Very many people know dissatisfaction with their bodies, and it is not your personal fault. Sara Ahmed writes about “comfort”: to be comfortable is to feel so at ease in your surroundings that the boundary between body and world almost disappears. But spaces, images and norms, for Ahmed, “take the shape” of some bodies in advance and not of others. If your body does not match that shape, you get the sense that it is “wrong,” although the problem is the narrowness of the frame. From this point of view, your dissatisfaction is largely a trace of these norms, not the truth about you. Ahmed does not call on you to love yourself urgently. But you can notice where your body feels freer — and gradually choose more such places, people and activities.
body_shame.practice: Recall a place or situation where your body feels free and not under evaluation. What is different there? Could you spend at least a little time there today?

illness.text: When the body lets you down, your familiar trust in it collapses, and fear, anger and exhaustion are legitimate here. Affect theory grew out of an idea of Spinoza’s that Deleuze and Massumi like to repeat: no one has yet determined what a body can do. For them, the body is not a machine that is either working or broken but a process, a capacity to affect and to be affected. This capacity changes: illness narrows some possibilities, but the body keeps searching for others — a different rhythm, different supports, different joys. From this point of view, illness does not cancel you: you remain a living field of relationships in which more than suffering is possible. This is no reason to demand resilience of yourself. Rather, it is an invitation to notice small changes — moments when things get a little easier — and to lean on them.
illness.practice: Note one moment today when your body felt even a little easier or more pleasant: warm tea, light, a comfortable position. Stay in it for a few breaths.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good feeling, and there is no need to hide it out of modesty. Silvan Tomkins considered the positive affects — interest and joy — not a pleasant addition to life but something worth consciously sustaining: they nourish curiosity and the capacity to act. Following him, Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick wrote about the close link between shame and pride: shame makes you hide your face, while pride lets you show it. Spinoza, from whose philosophy affect theory grew, called “self-contentment” the joy that arises when a person contemplates themselves and their own power of acting. From this point of view, your pride is not vanity but an opportunity to see your strength and not apologize for it. You can savor this joy without hurrying.
pride.practice: Tell someone about what you managed to do — or write it down — without caveats like “it’s nothing special.” Notice how this feels in your body.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow lives alongside tenderness. It needs neither to be driven away nor treated. In The Promise of Happiness, Sara Ahmed criticizes a culture that demands that we absolutely “be happy” and hurries us to “let go” of the past. She writes about the figure of the “melancholic migrant,” who is reproached for holding on to what was lost — and defends the right not to hurry. Ahmed also speaks of “the freedom to be unhappy”: the right to feelings that don’t fit into mandatory optimism. From this point of view, your melancholy is not a mood error but a way of gently holding on to what mattered. It doesn’t need fixing. You can simply listen to what exactly it remembers.
melancholy.practice: Sit with this mood for a couple of minutes without changing anything, and write down one thing it seems to be keeping safe in memory.
